concept.name: Call credit spread
concept.definition: A call credit spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short call at a lower strike and a long call at a higher strike, same underlying and same expiration, entered for a net credit. It is synonymous with the bear call spread: a moderately bearish-to-neutral position whose maximum gain is the credit received and whose maximum loss is the strike width minus the credit.
concept.intuition: You sell a call betting the stock stays below your strike, and buy a higher-strike call as a built-in stop so a rally cannot hurt you beyond a known amount.
concept.mechanics: The net credit is received at entry and kept in full if the underlying finishes at or below the short strike; the long call caps losses above the higher strike. The CFTC describes the call bear spread as purchasing the higher-strike call and selling the lower-strike call, same class and expiration.
concept.formula: Max gain = net credit; max loss = (K2 - K1) - net credit; breakeven = K1 + net credit, where K1 < K2 are the call strikes.
concept.failure_modes: Frequent small credits are punctuated by losses several times larger; gap-ups through both strikes realize maximum loss, and assignment of the short leg near expiration creates pin risk and possible residual stock positions.
concept.misconceptions: A high probability of keeping the credit is not the same as positive expectancy — the loss when wrong is a multiple of the credit, and the credit is payment for accepting that downside, not free income.
concept.example: Sell the XYZ $100 call for $4.00, buy the $105 call for $1.50: net credit $2.50. If XYZ finishes at or below $100, keep $250; at or above $105, lose $250.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
